opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most underappreciated questions in the field right now, because a lot of what gets called "continual learning" is evaluated in ways that don't really capture what we care about.

The classic setup comes from the older continual learning literature: you have a sequence of tasks, say permuted MNIST or split CIFAR, you train on them one after another, and you measure how much performance on earlier tasks degrades. That's catastrophic forgetting, and it's a real phenomenon, but for large language models I think that framing is too narrow. An LLM isn't just learning a sequence of disjoint classification tasks. What we actually want is a model that can keep absorbing new information, new skills, new contexts over time, and integrate them with what it already knows, without needing to be retrained from scratch.

So, a few things I think good evaluation needs.

First, we have to separate memorization from actual learning. If I show the model a new fact and then ask about that exact fact, that's a pretty weak test. The more interesting question is whether the model can use that new knowledge compositionally: reason with it, combine it with older knowledge, apply it in a different context. A lot of knowledge-editing benchmarks only test the direct recall case and maybe some paraphrases, and then the ripple effects are where things fall apart.

Second, we need to measure both sides of the stability-plasticity trade-off at the same time. It's easy to build a method that never forgets, because it barely learns anything new. And it's easy to build one that learns new things quickly but overwrites everything. Reporting only one side is misleading. You want to see forward transfer, backward transfer, and retention of general capabilities together.

Third, and this connects to my own work on memory architectures like Titans and the nested learning perspective, I think we should evaluate across different timescales. Some information should be held for a few tokens, some across a long context, some should be consolidated into the parameters permanently. A good continual learner should handle that whole spectrum. So long-context benchmarks, test-time learning or adaptation benchmarks, and longer-horizon settings where knowledge has to persist across sessions should be seen as points on the same continuum rather than separate research areas.

Fourth, efficiency has to be part of the evaluation. If your continual learning method requires replaying a large fraction of the original pretraining data, or storing a growing buffer forever, that's a valid baseline, but it doesn't really solve the problem. Compute and memory cost per update should be reported alongside accuracy.

And finally, I'd love to see more realistic, streaming-style evaluations. In the real world, data doesn't arrive in neatly labeled task boundaries. It's a continuous, non-stationary stream, and the model often doesn't know when the distribution has shifted. Benchmarks with explicit task IDs make the problem artificially easy.

So my short answer is: evaluate whether the model actually gets better and more useful over time in a realistic stream of experience, while staying efficient and keeping its general abilities, not just whether it avoids forgetting on a toy sequence of tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think this is actually one of the hardest parts of the whole area, and honestly I think a lot of the current evaluation is kind of broken.

The way most people evaluate continual learning right now is: you take a pretrained model, you fine-tune it on a sequence of tasks, and then you measure how much it forgot on the earlier tasks and how well it does on the new ones. And that's fine as a starting point, but it misses what we actually care about. If the real goal is a model that keeps learning from its experience at test time, the way a person does, then the evaluation has to look like that. You need settings where the model sees a long stream of information, where the distribution shifts over time, and where the relevant thing it needs to recall could be very far back in the stream. So long-context and needle-in-a-haystack style tasks are actually closer to the right spirit than people give them credit for, but they're still too static. The model should have to acquire something new, use it, and then still have it much later, without us explicitly telling it "this is a training phase, now this is a test phase."

The second thing I'd push on is that we should separate what the model memorizes from how it decides what's worth memorizing. A lot of forgetting is actually a storage problem, you only have so much capacity in the weights or in the memory, so the question is whether the model allocates that capacity to the surprising, useful stuff versus the redundant stuff. If your benchmark just rewards recalling everything, you're not really measuring that. I like evaluations where there's a lot of noise or distractor information in the stream, and the model gets credit for being selective.

And then third, I think we need to be honest about compute. It's easy to get good continual learning numbers by doing a lot of gradient steps at test time, but then you've just moved training into inference and the comparison to a transformer with a long context is not fair. So I'd want to see things like, at a fixed inference budget, at a fixed memory size, how does this architecture scale as the sequence gets longer and longer. That's where you actually see whether the learning mechanism is doing something that attention can't.

So in short: streaming settings with distribution shift, rewarding selectivity rather than raw recall, and controlling for compute. If a paper does those three things, I trust the result a lot more.

astra-6.text:
I think we should evaluate it as a process over time, rather than just asking, “What’s the score after training?” You have a model, you expose it to new information or new tasks, and you measure both what it learns and what happens to the capabilities it already had.

Forgetting is one part of that, but it’s not the whole problem. A model that never changes won’t forget anything, and it also won’t learn anything. So we need to measure how efficiently it acquires new knowledge, whether that knowledge transfers to other tasks, and whether it can update something that was previously true but is no longer true.

For LLMs, I’d also want to distinguish using information that’s sitting in the context from learning something that remains useful after that context is gone. Both are valuable, but they demonstrate different things.

And the resource budget matters. If you retain all the old data and retrain on everything, that’s a useful baseline, but we should account for the compute and storage it requires. The interesting question is whether a model can keep adapting over a long sequence of experiences, under a realistic budget, while preserving and building on what it already knows.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to evaluate learning as a process over time, rather than just evaluating a final checkpoint. If you train on one task, then another task, and measure how much of the first one you forgot, that’s useful, but it’s only part of the picture.

For LLMs, I would want to know: can the model acquire new information, retain useful prior knowledge, and use the two together? If something changes, can it update its understanding rather than simply memorize two contradictory answers? And does learning one thing make it easier to learn something related later?

The evaluation should also account for resources. If you retain all the previous data and retrain on everything, that’s a very different solution from a model that learns from a stream with limited memory and compute. We should compare those approaches under explicit budgets.

Ultimately, I’d like to see evaluations where the distribution keeps changing and we measure performance throughout that experience. That lets us distinguish a model that merely avoids forgetting from one that actually becomes a better learner.
